lesson.title: Averaging Both Sides for a Better Estimate
lesson.summary: The symmetric difference quotient estimates a derivative by averaging the forward and backward difference quotients, typically giving a far more accurate approximation than either one-sided estimate alone.
lesson.body:
The symmetric difference quotient is defined as [f(a+h) - f(a-h)] / (2h), and it can be understood as directly averaging the forward difference quotient [f(a+h) - f(a)] / h and the backward difference quotient [f(a) - f(a-h)] / h. Instead of stepping away from a in only one direction, it straddles the point, using one reading just ahead and one reading just behind. Intuitively, whatever error the forward estimate makes by overshooting the true slope tends to be canceled by the error the backward estimate makes by undershooting it, since both errors come from the same curvature of the function but enter with opposite signs when averaged together.

Revisit the position table from before: s(1) = 2, s(2) = 8, s(3) = 18, s(4) = 32, coming from s(t) = 2t^2 with true velocity s'(t) = 4t. Earlier, the backward difference at t = 2 gave 6 meters per second and the forward difference gave 10 meters per second, while the true velocity was 8. The symmetric difference quotient at t = 2, using h = 1, is [s(3) - s(1)] / (2)(1) = (18 - 2) / 2 = 16 / 2 = 8 meters per second. This matches the true derivative exactly, a dramatic improvement over either one-sided estimate, and it happens because the errors from the forward and backward directions, one too high, one too low, cancel out perfectly when averaged for this particular quadratic function.

This cancellation is not a coincidence specific to this one table. In general, the error in a one-sided difference quotient shrinks in proportion to h itself, while the error in the symmetric difference quotient shrinks in proportion to h squared, which is a much smaller quantity once h is small. That is why halving h roughly halves the error of a one-sided estimate but roughly quarters the error of a symmetric estimate, making the symmetric version the preferred choice whenever data exists on both sides of the point of interest.

There is an important caution, however: a symmetric difference quotient can exist and give a finite limit even at a point where the function is not actually differentiable, because the averaging can silently cancel a genuine mismatch. Take f(x) = |x| at a = 0, the corner point from earlier. For any h not equal to 0, f(h) - f(-h) = |h| - |h| = 0, so the symmetric difference quotient is 0 / (2h) = 0 for every single h, and its limit as h approaches 0 is 0. Yet f is not differentiable at 0, since the true one-sided derivatives are -1 and 1, not 0. The symmetry of the corner exactly cancels the mismatch that a genuine one-sided check would have caught.

The lesson is that the symmetric difference quotient is an excellent numerical tool for estimating derivatives from data, especially when a formula is unavailable, but it is not a substitute for the formal definition of the derivative when a rigorous conclusion about differentiability is required. It estimates well; it does not certify existence.
